extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, journal referees, and philosophers/sociologists of mathematical practice
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and norms used by research mathematicians and referees to judge whether an omitted step (a gap) in a published proof is acceptable. Draws on empirical interviews about refereeing practices and norms governing reasonable omission and signposting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitted step is routine for the intended audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The omitted step is a routine move that the intended readership is expected to be able to supply (e.g., a standard calculation, a textbook lemma, an obvious case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: standard calculation, textbook lemma, obvious case. Such routine omissions are more likely to be accepted by referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author reputation for reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's prior record of publishing correct proofs increases tolerance for gaps: established authors are given more benefit of the doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reputation functions legitimately in refereeing; referees treat papers by reliable authors as more acceptable even when gaps exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitted step is plausible at sight
rubrics_metrics.description: A gap is acceptable when the referee can see that 'something true and provable' lies in the omitted part even without tracing it in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees often skip steps they find plausible; plausibility is a default for gap-filling behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion is corroborated by other arguments or special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof's conclusion is more credible when it is supported by independent lines of argument or verifiable special cases that the referee can check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corroboration (e.g., special cases the referee can verify) makes gaps less worrying because the end-result is supported elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filling the gap is technically straightforward (but tedious)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gaps that are long, tedious, or repetitive calculations or case enumerations—i.e., technically straightforward—are acceptable if they do not conceal conceptual difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If filling the gap only requires bounded, routine effort (even if lengthy), referees accept omitting it rather than asking the author to write it out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gap is signposted by the author
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should mark where they omit work and indicate how it would be filled (so readers are not misled into thinking a skipped step is being claimed as proved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit signposting (e.g., 'the computation is omitted', or a reference) increases acceptability; lack of signposting harms trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gap hides the main idea (unacceptable)
rubrics_metrics.description: A gap is unacceptable when it conceals the central, load-bearing idea of the proof—that is, when the omitted part actually is the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the omitted material is where the central conceptual contribution lies, referees will regard the proof as insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gap occurs at a contested step or where intuition fails (unacceptable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps where the conclusion is contested, where common intuition is unreliable, or where errors are likely should not be left as gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees pay special attention to such steps; omissions here invite requests for full argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitted step requires a non-routine technique not signaled (unacceptable)
rubrics_metrics.description: When filling the gap would need a non-routine or specialized technique that the author has not indicated, the omission is unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should flag when a gap requires an unexpected method; failing to do so is misleading and undermines acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author has a history of errors or low community trust (unacceptable)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author (or the subfield) has a known history of mistakes or low trustworthiness, referees are less likely to accept gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community trust modulates tolerance: lower trust raises the burden for explicitness and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gap is unmarked or disguises a claim as 'clear' (unacceptable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unmarked omissions, or phrasing that disguises significant work as 'clear' or 'obvious', are judged poorly because they mislead readers about what has been established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly calling out omitted work is required; otherwise the omission is treated as a faulty presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Result depends sensitively on the gap (unacceptable)
rubrics_metrics.description: If small changes in the omitted argument would break the conclusion, the gap is not acceptable because the result is unstable without the detailed argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensitivity to the specifics of the omitted reasoning increases the need for a full argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees sample and prioritize (practical norm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees do not verify every line; they sample the proof and concentrate attention on steps that look most likely to harbor errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice explains why routine/ plausible gaps are tolerated while suspicious steps receive scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author is ultimately responsible for correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Normatively, the author bears responsibility for the correctness of the proof; referees aim to find serious problems but are not expected to certify every line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees' role is to detect significant flaws, not to reconstruct entire omitted developments; authors must provide what is necessary for verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gaps should be recoverable with bounded effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptable omissions are those a competent reader can reconstruct with bounded (reasonable) effort; gaps that force a reader to redo the author's work are unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical standard: the reader should not be required to perform the author's original derivation in full to understand the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gaps should not be concentrated at the load-bearing step
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof should not place multiple or critical omissions at the central step(s) that carry the argument's weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distributing omitted material away from the core idea (or fully detailing the core) preserves acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerous non-routine gaps (poorly written)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof containing many non-routine omissions for the intended audience is judged poorly: the cumulative burden on the reader is excessive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should avoid producing a proof that requires the reader to fill multiple substantial, specialized gaps.
